To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the signaled reinforcement effect on operant response rates and resistance is robust and is not dependent on the nature of the signal.

(i) the presence of a signal that accompanies reinforcement increases response resistance to extinction, prefeeding, or alternative reinforcement and (ii) the presence of an uncor related stimulus that accompanies reinforcement decreases response resistance to extinction or prefeeding.

(a) response rates and resistance are greater when reinforcement is signaled by an uncorrelated stimulus than when reinforcement is signaled with a response-produced stimulus and (b) response rates and resistances are greater when reinforcement occurs with a response-produced uncorrleated stimulus than when reinforcement occurs with no signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a stimulus signal on operant performance.
the effects of a brief signal on operant behavior.
understanding the role of the reinforcement contingency in the maintenance of behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reinforcement signal has an effect on the resistance to change, but this effect depends on the nature of the signal.
a response-produced unconditioned stimulus is not a necessary or sufficient condition for the production of resistance to change, but that it can produce it in some circumstances.
the effect of a signal on resistance to change is not a simple function of response rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reinforcement rate is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for resistance to change.

response resistance to change is greater when reinforcement is signaled by an uncorrelated stimulus or by a brief signal than when reinforcement is unsignaled, and that this effect occurs in the absence of a change in response rate.
response rate and resistance are affected by the presence or absence of a signal, and that these effects are related to the nature of the signal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
resistance to change is not a simple function of reinforcer rate.
the effects of a stimulus that accompanies a reinforcer can be quite different than the effects of a signal that is uncorrelated with reinforcement.
the presence of an uncorresponding signal may affect response rates in the absence of a signal-reinforcer contingency.
